chunks.text: There are many physical problems in which a body undergoes motion about a central point.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: And when that happens, there's a natural coordinate system to describe that motion, which

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: in two dimensions is polar coordinates.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: So let's consider the orbit of an object.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: For instance, the best example is the circular orbit.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: We have a circular orbit of an object.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: There is a central point, which we'll call P.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: Now, given this type of motion with an object, it naturally makes sense to choose a coordinate

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: system called polar coordinates.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: The way that coordinate system works is as follows.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: First off, we need to choose a reference angle, and so we'll choose a horizontal line,

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: and we'll draw a ray, and we'll show a direction of increasing reference angle theta.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: In this example, theta will go from 0 to 2 pi.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: Along with the reference angle, we have a distance from the central point, and that distance

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: will refer to as R. So the coordinates of our point are R and theta.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: Now the variable R is always greater than R, and can go to infinity, greater than 0.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: So this is our polar coordinate system.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: When you have a coordinate system, remember, at every point in space, there has to be unit

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: vectors.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: So at this point right here, how do we choose unit vectors for polar coordinates?

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: We always choose the unit vectors to point in the increasing direction of the coordinate.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: Take the R coordinate, that increases radially outward.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: So our unit vectors here will have a R hat pointing radially outward.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: What about the theta direction?

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: Tengential to the circle, in this particular case.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: Because theta is increasing in this direction, we choose our tangential unit vector, which

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: we're going to call theta hat, which is at right angles to R hat, to point in the direction

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: of increasing theta.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: And so at this point, we now have a set of unit vectors.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: Now one has to be very careful in polar coordinates for the following reason.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: Suppose that you're at another point over here.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: Now because we have two different points, let's just give some names to these points,

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: we'll call this S1 and this point S2.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: And the unit vectors over here, where R1 and theta1.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: When we're at the point S2, we have to choose unit vectors exactly the same way.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: R hat 2 points in the direction of increasing R, and theta hat 2 points in the direction

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: of increasing theta.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: So what we see in polar coordinates is that R hat 1 is not equal to R hat 2.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: Why are they not equal?

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: They both are unit vectors, so they both have the same magnitude.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: But they point in opposite directions in the same way that theta hat 1 is not equal

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: to theta hat 2.

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: So unlike Cartesian coordinates in which at every single point had the same unit vectors,

chunks.title: pully
chunks.text: in polar coordinates, the unit vectors depend on where you are in space.
